cards.title: The tablet nobody read
cards.prompt: The Abermule instruments were interlocked and Newtown had issued a correct tablet. Which tablet was the down train carrying when it left, who put it on the footplate, and what was the casualty list?
cards.body: The down train left holding the Montgomery–Abermule tablet — the one it had just surrendered, valid only for the section behind it. Relief-stationmaster Frank Lewis passed the pouch over without opening it. Both tablets pulled from the wreck were numbered 18. Head-on at about 12.6 p.m.: 17 killed, 36 injured.
cards.answer: The Montgomery–Abermule tablet, for the section it had just left; relief-stationmaster Frank Lewis handed it up without looking inside the pouch; 17 killed and 36 injured.

cards.title: John Owen, passed-fireman
cards.prompt: Both footplates were handed a tablet that morning. Name the fireman on the express, the routine he followed with his at Newtown that the down train's enginemen skipped, and what he went looking for while injured in the wreckage.
cards.body: At Newtown, foreman Brock handed Owen the Newtown–Abermule tablet. Owen examined it, found it correct, and passed it to driver John Pritchard Jones to examine before hanging the holder on the hook. Injured in the collision, he crept under a wrecked coach and recovered both tablet holders from beside the engines.
cards.answer: John Owen: he examined the tablet, satisfied himself it was correct, and had his driver examine it too before it went on the hook. Afterwards he crawled under the wreck to find both tablets.

cards.title: Ministry of Transport report on the collision at Abermule
cards.sub: Letter dated 8 April 1921 · Ministry of Transport · Railways Archive doc 103
cards.prompt: Name the primary document that carries the Abermule findings, who signed it and on what date, and the one piece of new equipment it recommended for single-line passing places.
cards.body: Signed J. W. Pringle, 8 April 1921, with the witnesses’ evidence attached. Its recommendation: electric interlocking between the single-line tokens and the starting, or advance starting, signal giving access to the section — wiring the token to the thing that admits the train.
cards.answer: The Ministry of Transport accident report, signed J. W. Pringle on 8 April 1921. It recommended electric interlocking between the single-line token and the starting or advance starting signal for the section.

cards.title: The check moves to the last hand
cards.sub: 1921 → the fencing token in your storage layer
cards.prompt: Abermule's fix added nothing to the interlock. Name the two places Pringle put the check instead, and the modern mechanism that makes exactly the same move for a distributed lock.
cards.body: Onto the person about to act — enginemen must examine the token before entering, and only the authorised person may handle it — and onto the gate itself, by interlocking the token with the signal admitting the train. Same shape as a fencing token the storage layer checks and refuses when stale.
cards.answer: Onto the last actor (the driver must read the token) and onto the resource (the signal is interlocked with the token). The modern equivalent is a monotonic fencing token enforced at the resource, not at the lock service.
